Robert Schumann. The German composer, pianist, and one of the most influential music critics of the Romantic era.

His music is characterized by its intense subjectivity, literary allusions, and flights of fantasy, particularly in his piano works and art songs known as Lieder. His career as a virtuoso pianist ended early after a hand injury, leading him to focus on composition and writing.

Schumann edited the highly influential journal Neue Zeitschrift für Musik, or New Journal for Music. He wrote reviews under the pseudonyms Florestan, representing his passionate, impetuous side, and Eusebius, his introspective, dreamy side.

He married Clara Wieck, a child prodigy and one of the most distinguished pianists of the nineteenth century. She became the champion and performer of his music. They married against her father's bitter opposition.

Carnaval is a set of twenty-one short piano pieces depicting a masked ball. It contains musical portraits of commedia dell'arte characters, his alter egos, Chopin, Paganini, and his beloved Clara.

Dichterliebe, or A Poet's Love, is his celebrated 1840 song cycle setting sixteen poems by Heinrich Heine. It is known for its psychological depth and extensive piano postludes.

His Symphony No. 3 in E-flat major is known as the Rhenish Symphony, inspired by a trip to the Rhineland. It has five movements, including a solemn fourth movement reflecting a cardinal's elevation inside Cologne Cathedral.

Schumann was the mentor of Johannes Brahms, the young composer whom he took in as a protégé. He famously proclaimed Brahms the future of music in his 1853 article Neue Bahnen, or New Paths.

Schumann is a central figure of German High Romanticism. He authored several complex piano sonatas. He attempted suicide by leaping into the Rhine River, reflecting the turbulent, romantic obsession with water and nature.

Tormented by severe mental illness, Schumann attempted suicide in 1854 and spent his final years in an asylum, where he died at age forty-six.
